passage:
"I got you a mango shake as well," Mridul said, sliding it across the canteen table.
"Thanks. Mridul, I can pay for my own."
"I know. But since your dad's job... I thought it would help."
"It does help. Kind of. But when you look at me like that, like I'm a sad story, it stings."
"Sorry. I didn't mean it like that."
"I know. Look, the notes you offered for maths, yes please. That's fair. Sharing a bench, fine. But paying for everything, no."
"Okay. Notes and no pity face?"
Eshaan laughed a little. "Deal. And thank you for the shake. I'll drink this one."
Mridul grinned, relieved. "Next time you buy."

qa.q: What did Mridul buy for Eshaan at the canteen?
qa.a: A mango shake.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan say the offer helped and stung at the same time?
qa.a: He was grateful for Mridul's kindness but his pride was hurt by being looked at like a sad story.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do that was wise in answering Mridul's help?
qa.a: He accepted what felt fair, like the maths notes and sharing a bench, and clearly said he did not want pity or everything paid for, without rejecting the kindness.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Eshaan told him the pity face stung?
qa.a: Probably a bit embarrassed and sorry, since he said sorry and hadn't meant it that way. He seems relieved when Eshaan laughs and agrees to a deal.

grounding: A friend's pity is kind but stings the protagonist's pride; he accepts fair help and says when he does not want pity.

passage:
Vinita: hey, you weren't at the bus stop. everything ok?
Tejas: yeah. Mum's shop closed down, so I walk now, it's fine
Vinita: oh. I'm sorry Tejas
Tejas: don't make it a thing pls 🙂
Vinita: I won't. Can I ask something small? I'm doing chemistry notes tonight, want to do them together? I'll come to the library
Tejas: you don't have to
Vinita: I want to. I'm also terrible at balancing equations 😅 you'd be doing me a favour
Tejas: haha ok. 5pm?
Vinita: 5pm. I'll bring the good biscuits. And I won't tell anyone, promise
Tejas: thanks Vinita ❤️

qa.q: Where will Vinita and Tejas study together?
qa.a: At the library, at 5pm.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say she is terrible at balancing equations, and what did she want?
qa.a: She wanted to offer company and notes in a way that did not make Tejas a charity case, so she framed it as him doing her a favour, while really wanting to help.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that helps Tejas, and what should she avoid?
qa.a: She offered time, notes and company and promised privacy. She should avoid gossiping about his family's trouble.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about Vinita's offer?
qa.a: Grateful and a little relieved. He first said she didn't have to, then agreed and thanked her with a heart, so her tone made it easy to accept.

grounding: A friend wants to help a struggling family by offering time and notes without making him a charity case.

qa.q: What is Jagdish sensing behind the compliments, and how does he feel about it?

passage: Sunday night. Salma here, and I don't know what to think. On Friday, Elizabeth from Class 6 stopped me in the corridor and asked how I plait my hair, then three of her friends copied the style on Saturday. They wave from across the ground. Someone asked for my old English notes like they were treasure. It feels really good, I won't lie. But today I caught myself checking who was watching before I answered a question in class, and I walked differently on the stairs. That's silly. I still can't parallel park a bicycle, and I failed the last science quiz. They think I have it all figured out. I don't. Tomorrow I'll tell Elizabeth that I'm still learning too.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask Salma about in the corridor?
qa.a: How she plaits her hair.

qa.q: Why was Salma uneasy about how she was acting, and what worried her?
qa.a: She caught herself checking who was watching before answering in class and walking differently on the stairs. She realised the attention was affecting how she acted.

qa.q: What could Salma do to keep her feet on the ground?
qa.a: Stay humble, be honest with the younger students that she is still learning, like they are, and not rely on the audience. 🙂

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Salma?
qa.a: As someone who has it all figured out. That's what Salma fears, since Elizabeth and her friends copy her style and treat her notes like treasure.

grounding: Younger students idolise the protagonist, which feels good but distorts her self-view; she resolves to stay humble.

passage:
Class teacher's note.

I have noticed that Nirmala has been eating lunch alone at the far end of the steps for about three weeks. Today I sat down near her. She said, quietly, that it hurts more than she lets on, and that she thinks no one would want to sit with her anyway. I told her that being alone right now isn't the same as being unlovable, and asked what she enjoys. Drawing, she said. I introduced her to Tenzin, who runs the art club, and he invited her on Thursday. She agreed to try one session. I will keep checking in and, if it doesn't ease, arrange time with the counsellor.

qa.q: Where has Nirmala been eating lunch?
qa.a: Alone at the far end of the steps.

qa.q: What did Nirmala reveal about her feelings, and what belief worried the teacher?
qa.a: That being alone hurts more than she lets on. She believes no one would want to sit with her, which is a belief the teacher wants to gently challenge.

qa.q: What small steps did the teacher take to help Nirmala?
qa.a: They sat near her, listened, asked what she enjoys, introduced her to Tenzin and the art club, and will involve the counsellor if it does not ease.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel about welcoming Nirmala?
qa.a: Probably glad to have another person who likes drawing. Inviting her to Thursday's session was a friendly, low-pressure way to begin.

grounding: An isolated student is helped to find an activity group and adult support instead of believing she is unlovable.

passage:
Dear Rajni Masi,

You asked why I have gone quiet on the phone. The truth is that some kids in my class call me weird, poor, and other things about my body. They do it when the teacher isn't looking, and sometimes they copy how I talk. Last week someone stuck a note on my bag. I cried in the washroom and hated myself for a while. But I have been thinking: nothing they say is my fault. Their words are about them. I've started spending lunch in the art room, where nobody cares what I wear. Yesterday I showed the note to my class teacher, and she said she would deal with it. I wanted you to know, because I'm not alone in this.

Love,
Jasleen

qa.q: Where has Jasleen started spending lunch?
qa.a: In the art room.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel at first, and how has her thinking changed?
qa.a: She cried in the washroom and hated herself for a while, but now she believes the mocking is not her fault and that their words are about them.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do that helps her in this situation?
qa.a: She protected her self-respect by not believing their story, found a place where she fits in the art room, and reported the harassment by showing the note to her teacher.

qa.q: How might Rajni Masi feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably sad and protective, but also proud that Jasleen spoke up. She asked why Jasleen had gone quiet, so she cares and will be glad to know.

grounding: The protagonist is mocked, refuses to believe the story, finds a place to fit in and reports the harassment.

passage: In the school computer lab, Eshaan had a tab open with Riya's holiday photos, then Kabir's football clips, then Jasmine's party. Everyone seemed to be laughing. He scrolled until the bell rang, feeling small. Mridul sir, the lab teacher, glanced at the screen as he shut down the computers. "Nice trip," he said mildly. "Whose?" "Just someone's," Eshaan muttered. Later he thought about Riya's post from last week, the one saying she couldn't sleep before exams. It had been buried under all the smiling pictures. He wasn't sure why the thought helped. He deleted the tabs, and signed up for the coding club that had been posted outside the lab for a month, even though it felt awkward.

qa.q: Who glanced at Eshaan's screen in the computer lab?
qa.a: Mridul sir, the lab teacher.

qa.q: How was Eshaan feeling as he scrolled through the photos, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He felt small and envious. Remembering Riya's post about not sleeping before exams showed him the smiling pictures hid worries too.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do with his envy?
qa.a: Notice that online pictures are curated, avoid tearing anyone down and build his own strengths, as he began by joining the coding club.

qa.q: How might Mridul sir see what Eshaan was doing?
qa.a: Probably as a student feeling left out. He mildly asked whose trip it was rather than scolding, which leaves space for Eshaan to talk if he chooses.

grounding: The protagonist envies popular classmates online, notices that curated images hide worries and turns to building his own strengths.

passage: Lucia's denim jacket was covered in patches she had sewn herself: a moth, a moon, a bus route from her grandmother's town in Valencia. At lunch in Madrid, everyone else wore the same white trainers. She liked being the odd one out, and said so. When Esther, the girl from her maths group, waved her over to the crowded table, Lucia said, "You all copy each other. I don't need that." Esther's smile faded. "I just thought you'd like the spare seat." Lucia ate alone, chin high, but the noise from the table stayed with her. On Friday she thought: is it really pride, or am I using it as a wall? The next day she sat down at the end of the table, the jacket still on.

qa.q: What was on Lucia's denim jacket?
qa.a: Patches she had sewn herself: a moth, a moon and a bus route from her grandmother's town in Valencia.

qa.q: Why might Lucia's pride in being different also be a wall, and how can you tell she thought so?
qa.a: Her remark to Esther pushed people away, and afterwards the noise from the table stayed with her. On Friday she asked herself whether it was pride or a wall.

qa.q: What would you advise Lucia to do so she keeps her individuality and connects with others?
qa.a: Enjoy being different but stay open to people, as she did by sitting at the end of the table with her jacket on. She can remain herself while making friends. 🙂

qa.q: How might Esther have felt when Lucia said they all copy each other?
qa.a: Hurt and a bit rejected. Her smile faded and she said she only thought Lucia would like the spare seat.

grounding: The protagonist is proud to be different but sees that superiority can shield her from connection and stays open to others.

passage: Siddharth knew which stories made people lean in. In the hostel common room, he mentioned that Arun had failed the maths test, with a shrug, as if he pitied him, and three boys laughed and made room for him on the sofa. It worked again the next week. He was invited to the football group chat and everyone knew his name. But Pradeep, his roommate, went quiet. One night Pradeep said, "I stopped telling you things. I saw what happened to Arun's story." Siddharth lay awake. He had a full sofa and nobody he could talk to. On Saturday he told Arun he was sorry, and joined the football trials on his own merit, instead of by telling stories.

qa.q: What did Siddharth mention about Arun in the common room?
qa.a: That Arun had failed the maths test.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth lie awake after Pradeep spoke?
qa.a: He realised his gossip had won him a place on the sofa but had cost him trust; he felt hollow, with a full sofa and nobody he could talk to.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do to belong in an honest way?
qa.a: Apologise to those he hurt, as he did with Arun, and find belonging through real interests like the football trials rather than gossip and charm.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see Siddharth's habit?
qa.a: As a reason not to trust him. Pradeep said he stopped telling him things after seeing what happened to Arun's story, so he is protecting himself.

grounding: The protagonist climbs the social ladder with charm and gossip, feels hollow and chooses honest ways to belong.

passage:
"Why are you talking like Karan bhaiya now?" Vinita asked.
"Like what?"
"'Bro, that's literally so basic.' You've said it six times since dinner."
"He's cool, Didi. Everyone in school wants to be around him."
"Fine, he's cool. What did you do at lunch today?"
"I sat at Karan bhaiya's table."
"And Sameer?"
Rafiq paused. "He was sitting alone. I pretended I didn't see."
"Rafiq. Take what you like from Karan, the way he speaks up in class, his football. But don't drop Sameer or leave your own voice behind to get his attention."
"...I know."
"Go sit with Sameer tomorrow."
Rafiq exhaled. "Okay. I'll ask him about the match."

qa.q: What phrase did Vinita say Rafiq had repeated six times since dinner?
qa.a: "Bro, that's literally so basic."

qa.q: Why did Rafiq pretend he didn't see Sameer sitting alone, and how does he seem to feel about it?
qa.a: He wanted to fit in at Karan bhaiya's table and earn his notice, but his pause and "I know" suggest he feels guilty.

qa.q: What did Vinita advise Rafiq to do about Karan and Sameer?
qa.a: Take what inspires him from Karan, keep his own voice, and not drop his old friend Sameer. Go sit with Sameer tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Sameer have felt seeing Rafiq at Karan bhaiya's table?
qa.a: Probably hurt and left out, since he was sitting alone and Rafiq pretended not to see him.

grounding: The protagonist idolises a popular senior and copies him; an older sibling urges him to build his own voice and keep old friends.
